abstract: Post-extractive decline is commonly analysed through mine closure, employment loss, economic contraction and associated social disruption. Less attention has been given to how unresolved disruption remains socially consequential after the originating event has receded and across generations that did not directly experience it. Drawing on qualitative research with ninety-five women in Matjhabeng Local Municipality in South Africa’s Free State Goldfields, this paper examines the temporal afterlife of extractive decline. It develops Complex Economic Intergenerational Trauma (CEIT) as an explanatory mechanism through which economic and institutional rupture is absorbed, normalised and transmitted through the interaction of structural inheritance and interpretive transmission. The findings show that extractive decline persists not only through diminished material opportunities but through frameworks through which institutional withdrawal and subsequent institutional encounters are understood. The paper extends Social Disruption Theory from an account of rupture and its consequences towards an explanation of how disruption can acquire an intergenerational afterlife. CEIT distinguishes this process from persistent poverty or intergenerational disadvantage by locating transmission in an unresolved economic and institutional rupture whose material consequences and social meanings remain active over time. Derived from the Matjhabeng case, CEIT is advanced as an explanatory mechanism for comparative testing across post-extractive territories.
title: Post Extractive Afterlives through a Gendered Lens: Theorising Intergenerational Transmission

abstract: How households’ inflation expectations affect their spending is a central question for researchers and policymakers alike. Yet empirical evidence remains mixed. This column shows that the consumption question researchers choose can change the sign and strength of the estimated relationship. Questions about spending attitudes and plans yield negative associations with expected inflation, while questions about past spending yield weakly positive or insignificant associations. Differences in question type matter much more than reference unit or recall horizon. Treating these measures as interchangeable can lead to misleading conclusions about the expectations channel of monetary policy.
authors: Tiziana Assenza, Stefanie Huber, Anna Mogilevskaja, Tobias Schmidt
title: When wording changes what we find: The impact of inflation expectations on spending
